why: Hand derivation from the evidence alone; every interval below is cited. BERTH CLEARS. Cape Ferrol has 58 moves left at 16:30 (e5) and is worked to completion, not sailed short (e5). Four cranes give 92 gross moves per hour (e6). Gangs work to 17:00, break unworked 17:00-18:00, and the accepted four-gang order resumes the same four cranes at 18:00 (e7). From 16:30 to 17:00 is half an hour at 92/h = 46 moves, leaving 12; those 12 take 12/92 h = 7.8 min from 18:00, so the last container lands at about 18:08. (Deveaux's 18:10 is explicitly his estimate, not a measurement (e8); the computed figure governs and the two agree to within two minutes.) Lashing takes 40 min from the landing of the last container (e9) = 18:48. Unmooring may not begin until BOTH lashing is complete AND the pilot is aboard, whichever is later (e9); the outbound pilot was ordered for 19:00 (e10), so 19:00 governs. All lines gone 19:00 + 25 min = 19:25 (e9); stern clear of the berth face 10 min later = 19:35 (e9). Okafor observes the stern clear and is the only person who may declare the berth clear (e12); the declaration reaches the dispatcher within about 2 min (e13) = 19:37. TIDAL WINDOW. Rhine Meridian draws 45 ft 03 in, over the 44 ft trigger, so Standing Order 12 confines commencement of the inbound transit to 2h00m before through 0h30m after high water: high water 19:58, window 17:58 to 20:28 (e2, e3). Standing Order 9 additionally bars commencement until the berth is confirmed clear (e2), which happens at 19:37 -- inside the window with 51 minutes to spare. Neither order is waivable and no waiver was filed (e2). Even on the most conservative reading, where nothing at all is prepared before 19:37, heaving eight shackles takes about 30 min from the order and the run to the sea buoy about 15 min (e13), reaching the sea buoy at about 20:22, still inside the window. On the ordinary reading the pilot was ordered for 19:00 (e10), Beaudry is off rest and first on the board (e11), the ship is on immediate notice with a manned bridge answering VHF at once (e1), so the anchor is at short stay and the pilot on the bridge before 19:37 and the sea buoy is crossed at about 19:52. DOCKING. Inbound transits of this class average 3h05m from the sea buoy to all lines fast, inclusive of tug rendezvous and swinging at Kings Island (e14). That gives all fast at about 22:57 on the ordinary reading, or about 23:27 on the conservative one. Tugs are confirmed for 22:15 and line handlers rostered from 22:15 to 01:00, so neither constrains the docking (e14); weather and the two-way passage rule impose no bar (e15). Both readings put all fast at Berth 8 before the 23:59 deadline, so the answer is yes. THE NAIVE WRONG ANSWER IS 'no' by two distinct routes. First, concluding that a berth that only clears at 19:37 cannot make a window closing at 20:28 and that the vessel must therefore wait at Tybee Roads for the 06:31 window on 14 August -- which the resolution note names explicitly as a NO. That misses that the transit need only COMMENCE inside the window, and commencement clears it by roughly six minutes even under the worst assumption. Second, taking Deveaux's 18:10 projection as a measured fact and then treating the 17:00-18:00 break as additional delay on top of it, pushing the whole chain an hour later and out of the tide. The break is already accounted for in the 18:08 computation, and in any case the 19:00 pilot order, not the lashing, is what governs the start of unmooring.
